title: String Immutability and the Cost of Concatenation
summary: Why strings are immutable in most languages, why that turns naive loop concatenation into a hidden O(n²), and the buffer-based fix every mainstream language ships under a different name.

slides.markdown:
In Python, Java, JavaScript, C#, and most mainstream languages, **strings are immutable**: once created, a string's contents never change. Every operation that looks like a modification — `s += x`, `s.replace(...)`, `s.upper()` — actually builds a brand new string and leaves the old one untouched.

That's invisible when you do it once. It becomes an O(n²) bug the moment you do it n times in a loop, because each `+=` copies everything accumulated so far, not just the new piece.

This topic is about spotting that hidden cost and the one-line fix every language provides for it.

slides.subTitle: s += x allocates and copies, every time
slides.markdown:
`s += x` looks like it appends to `s`. What it actually does: allocate a new block of memory sized `len(s) + len(x)`, copy every byte of `s` into it, copy every byte of `x` after it, then repoint the variable `s` at the new block. The old block becomes garbage.

Nothing about the original string object changes — it can't, by definition of immutable. The variable `s` just now refers to a different, larger object.

So a single `+=` isn't O(1); it's O(current length of s). That single fact is the seed of everything else in this topic.

slides.sectionTitle: Why strings are immutable at all
slides.markdown:
Immutability isn't an accident of language design — it buys three things most programs rely on constantly:

- **Safe as a hash key.** A dict/hash-map key's hash must never change while it's stored, or the map breaks. A mutable string could be hashed, inserted, then edited — corrupting the map silently.
- **Safe to share without copying.** Passing a string to a function or another thread needs no defensive copy, because nothing can mutate it out from under the caller. This is what makes string interning possible: identical literals can safely share one object.
- **Safe as a cache/dictionary of itself.** Small, frequently used strings (short identifiers, single characters) get interned and reused across the whole program, saving memory — safe only because nobody can change one copy and affect another.

Mutable strings (`char[]` you own directly, C's raw buffers) give up all three in exchange for in-place edits — which is exactly why security-sensitive code (password buffers) often prefers mutable char arrays, so the memory can be explicitly zeroed after use.

slides.sectionTitle: Building a string with += in a loop
slides.markdown:
Run `s += chunk` n times and you don't get n cheap appends — you get n allocations, and each one copies more than the last, because `s` keeps getting longer.

<<< Image: a sequence of n string blocks stacked left to right, each one visibly wider than the last (lengths 1, 2, 3, ... n units); an arrow under each block showing "copy this much" with the copied region growing each time, ending in a bracket labelled "total copying = 1+2+3+...+n" >>>

The first `+=` copies a handful of characters. The thousandth copies everything built so far. The cost of the loop isn't n times the cost of one iteration — it's the sum of a steadily growing cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Why that adds up to O(n²)
slides.subTitle: The triangular sum of copy costs
slides.markdown:
If each chunk is roughly constant length, the string's length after k iterations is proportional to k. The k-th `+=` copies roughly k units of data. Summing that over n iterations:

```
1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2
```

That's the classic **triangular number**, which is Θ(n²). Ten iterations costs 55 units of copying; a hundred costs 5,050; a thousand costs about 500,000 — quadratic growth from what reads like a linear loop.

This is the same shape as the naive O(n·k) shift in array-shifting problems and the O(n²) brute-force range sum elsewhere in this group — a linear-looking loop whose per-iteration cost itself grows with the loop counter.

slides.sectionTitle: Missing the O(n²) hiding in plain sight
slides.markdown:
The reason this bug survives code review so often: **every individual `+=` looks like O(1).** There's no visible loop-within-a-loop, no nested iteration — just one line, executed n times.

`for word in words: result += word` reads exactly like an O(n) pass over `words`. It isn't, because the cost of each line depends on how large `result` has already grown, and that dependency is invisible in the syntax.

The tell in practice: string-building loops that are "mysteriously slow" past a few thousand items, and profile flat until you look at cumulative time spent inside string allocation — not any one line, but line after line each taking a little longer than the one before it.

slides.sectionTitle: += in a loop vs a buffer joined once
slides.markdown:
| Approach | Per-append cost | Total for n appends |
|---|---|---|
| `result += chunk` each iteration | grows with current length | O(n²) |
| append to a mutable buffer, join once at the end | amortized O(1) | O(n) |

The difference isn't the total amount of data written — both approaches write the same total characters. The difference is **how many times each character gets copied**: with `+=`, an early character gets recopied on every subsequent iteration; with a buffer, each character is written once and read once, at the final join.

```python
# O(n^2): result grows and gets fully re-copied on every iteration
def build_naive(words):
    result = ""
    for w in words:
        result += w        # copies everything accumulated so far
    return result

# O(n): each word is appended once, joined into one string once
def build_fast(words):
    parts = []
    for w in words:
        parts.append(w)     # amortized O(1), no copy of prior content
    return "".join(parts)   # one O(n) pass over all parts combined
```

On 100,000 words, `build_naive` does on the order of 5 billion character copies; `build_fast` does on the order of the total character count once. Same output, different order of magnitude in work.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the buffer approach is O(n)
slides.markdown:
A mutable buffer (Python's `list`, Java's `StringBuilder`, a growable char array) is exactly the dynamic array from earlier in this group: appending writes into pre-allocated capacity and is amortized O(1), because the buffer only reallocates and copies occasionally, not on every append.

The join step at the end is a single O(n) pass: walk the collected pieces once and write each character exactly once into the final string. No piece gets copied twice.

Total cost: O(n) for the amortized appends, plus O(n) for the final join — O(n) overall, versus O(n²) for repeated immutable concatenation.

Every mainstream language ships this exact fix, just under a different name:

- **Java / C#** — `StringBuilder` (`.append()`, then `.toString()`)
- **Python** — a `list` of pieces plus `"".join(parts)`
- **JavaScript** — an array of pieces plus `parts.join("")`, or template-literal accumulation which V8 optimizes internally with ropes
- **C++** — `std::string` itself is mutable and supports efficient `+=` via its own amortized-growth buffer, so the naive loop is *not* quadratic there — immutability is the language-specific trigger for this bug, not a universal one

The underlying idea is identical everywhere: never repeatedly rebuild an immutable value in a loop; accumulate into something mutable, then convert once.

slides.sectionTitle: The quadratic bug hides outside obvious loops too
slides.markdown:
The same pattern shows up disguised as something that doesn't look like a string-building loop at all:

- **Logging in a hot path** — building a log line with `msg = msg + f"{key}={value}, "` across many fields, called on every request.
- **Recursive tree serialization** — a function that returns `left_str + node_str + right_str` at every level, where each parent re-concatenates strings its children already built, silently re-copying the same characters at every level of recursion.
- **Report/HTML generation** — appending row after row of markup to one big string instead of a list of rows joined once.

The common thread: any place that repeatedly extends an immutable string across an unbounded number of calls is a candidate, whether or not there's a `for` keyword nearby.

slides.subTitle: When += in a loop isn't actually quadratic
slides.markdown:
A senior-level caveat: some compilers and interpreters special-case the pattern `s = s + x` (or `s += x`) when they can prove `s` has exactly one reference and isn't aliased elsewhere, rewriting it to an in-place resize-and-append under the hood. CPython does this for `str` concatenation in specific bytecode patterns (`BINARY_OP` with a sole reference), and some JIT compilers do the same.

This optimization is real but **not something to rely on**: it depends on reference counts, doesn't apply across all code paths (a string stored in a list or passed to a function loses the single-reference guarantee), and doesn't exist at all in many languages or contexts. Writing the explicit buffer-and-join version is correct in every language, every time, and costs nothing extra to write — so it's the version to reach for, treating any compiler optimization as a bonus rather than a plan.
